question: How many different remainders can result when the \(100\)th power of an integer is divided by \(125?\)
solution:
Separate integers divisible by \(5\) from the others. If \(5\mid N\), then \(125=5^3\) divides \(N^{100}\), so the remainder is \(0\).

Otherwise, \(N\) has remainder \(1,2,3,\) or \(4\) modulo \(5\). Their squares have remainders \(1,4,4,1\), respectively. Thus
\[
N^2=5m+\varepsilon
\]
for an integer \(m\) and \(\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}\). By the binomial theorem,
\[
N^{100}=(5m+\varepsilon)^{50}
=\varepsilon^{50}+50\varepsilon^{49}(5m)
+\binom{50}{2}\varepsilon^{48}(5m)^2+\cdots.
\]
The constant term is \(\varepsilon^{50}=1\). The next two terms are
\[
250\varepsilon m
\quad\text{and}\quad
1225\cdot25m^2=30625m^2,
\]
both divisible by \(125\). Every later term contains at least \((5m)^3\), so it is also divisible by \(125\). Therefore every integer not divisible by \(5\) gives remainder \(1\).

Both remainders occur, for example with \(N=5\) and \(N=1\). There are \(\boxed{2}\) possible remainders, choice \(\text{B}\).
